sections.html:
A South Carolina landlord can end a residential tenancy only after the right written notice, and the number of days depends on the reason. The main rules are in Title 27, Chapter 40 of the state code. The court steps are in Chapter 37.

SituationNotice or wait
Rent unpaid (27-40-710(B))5 days after the due date, plus written notice of nonpayment and intent to terminate
Other lease breach (27-40-710(A))Written notice; ends at least 14 days after receipt if not fixed in 14 days
Health and safety violation (27-40-720)14 days after written notice, or promptly in an emergency
Month-to-month tenancy (27-40-770(b))30 days written notice
Week-to-week tenancy (27-40-770(a))7 days written notice

Rent that is still unpaid five days after the due date lets the landlord terminate, after written notice of the nonpayment and the intent to terminate. A single notice covers the whole lease term. So does bold, clear language in the written lease itself.

When the lease carries that wording, no separate notice is needed to start an eviction, even after the original term ends on a month-to-month tenancy. In the ejectment chapter, the five-day period counts as legal notice for a residential lease only if the written agreement states it in bold, conspicuous type.

The landlord may recover actual damages and ask for injunctions, judgments or evictions in magistrate or circuit court with no bond. Attorney's fees are available only when an attorney represents the landlord and the nonpayment was not in good faith.

sections.h2: A lease violation that has nothing to do with rent
sections.html:
For any other breach, the landlord delivers a written notice naming each one. Termination lands no sooner than 14 days after the tenant gets the notice, and only if the problem is still there after 14 days. Cure it by the notice date and the lease stays alive.

Some repairs take longer. A tenant who starts the remedy inside the 14 days and pursues it in good faith avoids termination. Health and safety violations under Section 27-40-720 follow a similar 14-day path, and the landlord may enter to repair and bill the tenant when repair, replacement or cleaning will solve the problem.

  • Name the specific breach in writing
  • Keep proof of the day the tenant received the notice
  • Record any repair the tenant begins within the 14 days
  • Leave the locks and utilities alone, because Section 27-40-760 bars taking possession by action or otherwise outside the listed cases

sections.h2: Magistrate court after the notice period
sections.html:
The landlord files in magistrate court. The magistrate issues a written rule telling the tenant to vacate or show cause why they should not be ejected, and the tenant has ten days after service to answer.

A tenant who neither appears nor shows cause within that time faces a warrant of ejectment, carried out by a constable or the sheriff. A tenant who contests gets a hearing like any civil case, and either side can demand a jury.

  • Landlord wins: a writ of ejectment issues within five days.
  • Tenant wins: the tenant remains in possession until the tenancy ends by agreement or law, rent goes unpaid, or another proceeding ejects them.
  • Appeal: the ejectment goes ahead unless the tenant posts an appeal bond set by the magistrate. Miss the five-day bond deadline after service of the notice of appeal and the appeal is thrown out.

No statute fixes a day count for the hearing itself, so call the magistrate's office in your county for current scheduling.

sections.h2: Serving a tenant who is hard to find
sections.html:
The rule to show cause goes out by the usual summons methods, with backups when nobody answers. After two failed attempts at least 48 hours apart, at times at least eight hours apart, it may be affixed to the premises with documentation and mailed.

Mailed service counts ten days after the mailing date, so the ten-day show-cause period starts on the eleventh day. If the premises have sat abandoned for 15 days or more before service, the rule may be posted on the most conspicuous part of the building.

Abandonment has its own triggers. An unexplained absence of 15 days after a rent default is treated as abandonment, and a tenant who voluntarily ended the utilities has abandoned at once.

sections.h2: When the sheriff carries out the writ
sections.html:
The officer presents the writ and gives everyone inside 24 hours to leave. If they refuse, a deputy sheriff, though not a constable, may force entry using the least destructive means.

When the home looks occupied but nobody answers, a copy of the writ goes on the door or another conspicuous spot, and after 24 hours a deputy may force entry. The officer may delay removing ill or elderly tenants.

The eviction notice must warn the tenant that belongings left on a public street may be removed by officials after 48 hours, not counting Saturdays, Sundays and holidays. Property left after abandonment worth $500 or less may be disposed of by the landlord. Anything above that falls under Sections 27-37-10 to 27-37-150.

A landlord may not take possession through self-help, including interrupting essential services, except on abandonment, surrender or termination, or as the chapter permits.

Section 27-40-910 also bars retaliation. Once a tenant complains to a housing code agency or to the landlord about a violation of the chapter, the landlord may not raise rent above fair market value, cut essential services or bring a possession action, apart from listed exceptions.

A tenant who is wrongfully dispossessed can sue for damages under Section 27-37-140. Rent keeps accruing at the old rate while the tenant stays after proceedings start, and the landlord keeps the right to eject after accepting rent.

sections.h2: Selling a rental while an eviction is pending
sections.html:
You can sell during an eviction, but the notice, the court case and the tenant's rights do not vanish at closing. If the sale is made in good faith to a bona fide purchaser and the tenant is told in writing, the former landlord is released from liability for what happens afterward.

You remain on the hook for the security deposit until it is handed to the buyer and the tenant is notified in writing. A holdover can also cost money. If the stay is a wilful violation, the landlord may recover up to three months of periodic rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees.

  • An occupied house with a notice already served
  • A tenant who stopped paying months ago
  • A landlord who wants out before a court date
  • Heirs who inherited a house with a lease in place

We buy houses as-is, including with tenants in place, so you may not need to finish the eviction first. Tell us where the notice or case stands when you call, and keep every notice, receipt and court paper for the closing.

faqs.q: How many days is a South Carolina eviction notice for nonpayment?
faqs.a: Five days after the rent due date, followed by written notice of nonpayment and intent to terminate, or conspicuous language in the written lease. One notice covers the lease term.

faqs.q: How much notice ends a month-to-month tenancy in South Carolina?
faqs.a: Thirty days of written notice, given before the termination date. Week-to-week tenancies need seven days, under Section 27-40-770.

faqs.q: How long does the tenant have to respond to the court?
faqs.a: The tenant has ten days from service of the rule to show cause. If the tenant does not show cause, the magistrate issues a warrant of ejectment.

faqs.q: Can a landlord change the locks to evict a tenant?
faqs.a: No. Section 27-40-760 bars taking possession by action or otherwise, including by interrupting essential services, except on abandonment, surrender or termination or as the chapter permits.

faqs.q: Does selling the house end the lease?
faqs.a: Not by itself. Not on its own. A good-faith sale to a bona fide purchaser frees the seller from later liability once the tenant is told in writing, though the seller still answers for the deposit until it is transferred and the tenant knows.
